title: FEATURE: Japan's "Donut Man" builds lasting bond with Nepal quake village - Japan Wire by Kyodo News
description: FEATURE: Japan's "Donut Man" builds lasting bond with Nepal quake village  Japan Wire by Kyodo News
publisher.title: Japan Wire by Kyodo News
full_article:
Morihiko Shimamura, 68, has returned every year to Musure, a mountain village of about 500 people near the epicenter of the quake that killed around 9,000, bringing stationery and Japanese "randoseru" school satchels for local children.

Known affectionately there as the "Donut Man," Shimamura is expected to take up the post at a Japanese-language school for working adults in the Nepalese capital as early as next spring.

His path to Nepal can be traced through two of Japan's most devastating natural disasters.

"I thought a plane had crashed in a nearby park," Shimamura recalled of the morning of the Great Hanshin Earthquake on Jan. 17, 1995.

Originally from Osaka, he was living in Kawanishi, Hyogo Prefecture, when the quake struck. He later moved to Iwaki, Fukushima Prefecture, while working for a credit card company before leaving his job to start a business selling all-electric home products.

Then came the March 2011 earthquake and tsunami that ravaged northeastern Japan.

Amid a push for renewable energy following the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear disaster, Shimamura began handling solar panels and became involved in installing them at schools and supporting developing countries.

His connection with Nepal began in May 2015 during a visit to an elementary school in Aizuwakamatsu, Fukushima Prefecture.

A fourth-grade boy, who had lost his mother in the 2011 tsunami and evacuated from the town of Okuma, approached him with a request: he wanted to send solar panels to Nepal, which had been struck by a massive earthquake the previous month.

"My rule is that if someone asks me for help, I don't say no," Shimamura said.

Moved that a child who had endured such loss was thinking of others, Shimamura decided to act.

Although he had no connections in Nepal, he traveled there with support from "Fumbaro Nepal" (Hang in there, Nepal!), a project launched by the late Japanese mountaineer Nobukazu Kuriki.

Shimamura carried solar panels and batteries into mountain villages without electricity and taught residents how to connect them, bringing light to remote communities where wild tigers sometimes appear.

In another settlement, Musure, he encountered a young girl asking for water. Seeing how quickly she drank, Shimamura assumed she was hungry and gave her a doughnut he happened to be carrying.

The girl divided it into four pieces, sharing it with younger children around her before handing the remaining piece back to Shimamura.

Touched by her generosity, he decided he would maintain a lasting relationship with the village.

Shimamura has since returned annually with school supplies and randoseru. Villagers began calling him The Donut Man, and doughnuts are now sold at Musure's only shop as a symbol of their bond.

Children who once described a single pencil as a treasure have developed a love of school, while the village's small elementary school is now set to become a combined elementary and junior high school.

"I don't think about the reasons something can't be done. I just act," Shimamura said. "That's all there is to it."

Word of his work eventually reached people connected with the Kathmandu school, where he is expected to become principal next spring.

"I want to support young people hoping to go to Japan by helping them understand things like the cultural differences," he said.

title: Can Nepal protect Yomari? - kathmandupost.com
description: Can Nepal protect Yomari?  kathmandupost.com
publisher.title: kathmandupost.com
full_article:
Every year, as the month of November-December arrives, the sweet fragrance of steamed rice flour and warm chaku or khuwa fill drifts through the narrow lanes of Bhaktapur, Kathmandu and Lalitpur.

Newa families come together to form small fish-shaped dumplings, known as Yomari , from freshly harvested rice, filled with sesame seeds, coconuts, chaku or khuwa , prepared in a ritual that dates back centuries.

The festival for this food, called Yomari Punhi , is not just a cultural celebration; it is the embodiment of an agricultural knowledge system, linking a particular community, a particular crop, and a particular season.

However, if any foreign food company started producing Yomari today and began labeling it in a supermarket in another country, Nepal would have no legal means to prevent it , as there is no law, no registry, and no enforcement mechanism.

Nepal has 59 officially recognised indigenous nationalities called Adivasi Janajati, comprising around 35 percent of the total population. These span all the ecological zones.

Every community has its own identity, not only in its language and clothing but also in the way it grows its food, prepares its meals, weaves, carves, and heals. Their identity is inseparable from their products.

And yet, while Nepal has precise data on the number of its indigenous communities, it has almost no systematic data on what those communities actually produce.

There is no comprehensive national registry of traditional foods, no catalogue of indigenous medicinal herbs and their community custodians, and no documented inventory of craft techniques and their geographic distribution. Nepal knows it has 59 indigenous nationalities, but it does not know, in any legally useful sense, what those nationalities make, how they make it, or what makes it irreplaceable. A country cannot protect what it has not documented.

Researchers and institutions have identified over 100 agricultural products and 87 potential products that would qualify for international protection as Geographical Indications, a form of intellectual property that protects products whose quality or reputation is tied to a specific geographic origin.

Post file photo

But identification is not documentation. Information about Ilam Tea does not carry the same value as having a legally binding record of its growing altitude, the soil’s characteristics that affect its muscatel taste, and the traditional tea-making processes of the communities who grow it in Ilam. That documentation is required for registration.

For example, compare Yomari with Rasgulla, a centerpiece of one of India’s most famous Geographical Indication disputes, the syrup-soaked cottage cheese ball. The origin of Rasgulla has been disputed for years between West Bengal and Odisha. In 2017, West Bengal was awarded the Geographical Indications status for Banglar Rosogolla, and in 2019, Odisha was awarded the status of GI for Odisha Rasgola, acknowledging the two as separate products from different traditions. Each state’s producers were legally recognised, allowing them to mark their products as authentic, prevent imitations, and establish a market identity tied to their provenance.

Yomari is Nepal’s Rasgulla.

It has a specific community origin, a geographic tie, a centuries-old preparation tradition, and an international diaspora market that already recognises and values it. The difference is that West Bengal and Odisha had a legal system in which to file their claims. Nepal does not.

The same logic applies across Nepal’s entire indigenous product landscape, like Juju Dhau , the King of Yogurt, made in Bhaktapur.

Jumli Marshi rice is grown in Jumla, at an altitude of 2,000-2,900 metres, and depends on the unique flavour and nutritional characteristics of the extreme temperature variations and soil conditions provided by the Karnali region to make it the world’s tallest rice. The weaving density and pattern combinations of Palpali Dhaka fabric are linked to the weaving knowledge tradition practiced by the artisans of Palpa.

Khukuri knives, made by the blacksmith communities in Bhojpur, are known worldwide as a symbol of Nepali craftsmanship due to their curved shape and the steel tempering they undergo. Sherpa, Tamang, and Tibetan Buddhist communities use mineral pigments in a hand-ground technique and iconometric precision to create thangka paintings that are available in international art markets at prices that reflect centuries of value. All these products are potential GI products but are not registered due to the absence of law.

Every community has its own identity, not only in its language and clothing but also in the way it grows its food, prepares its meals, weaves, carves, and heals. Their identity is inseparable from their products.

Geographical Indication is the most appropriate legal tool for addressing this. Unlike a patent, it does not require novelty, nor does it require individual authorship as copyright does, nor can it be sold away from the community that owns it, as with a trademark. A GI belongs to all qualified producers in a defined geographic area who meet the production standards.

It is the only form of intellectual property designed for knowledge that is communal, intergenerational, and geographically rooted. And it is the only instrument that connects indigenous communities directly to international markets based on authenticated origin.

The market argument is not abstract. Across international commodity markets, GI-registered products consistently command price premiums over comparable non-registered alternatives. Darjeeling Tea, India’s first GI registration in 2004, commands a price of five to twelve times that of generic Indian black tea in European and Japanese specialty markets.

The Tea Board of India has registered the Darjeeling certification mark in roughly 30 countries. Ilam Tea, grown in ecologically comparable conditions sixty kilometers across the border, is exported to the same markets at a fraction of the price because Nepal has no equivalent certification system.

The farmers of Ilam are not producing an inferior product. They are producing an uncertified one. Nepal’s National Pashmina Sector Export Strategy aims to achieve an export volume of USD75 million in Pashmina by 2026, up from USD15 million in 2023-24.

The goal cannot be accomplished by marketing alone, once the term ‘Pashmina’ has become a generic name for machine-spun blended fiber available in airport stores in Asia and Europe. The only instrument that can restore the word to its authentic meaning and protect that meaning in law is GI registration backed by active enforcement.

This is why the Industrial Property Bill, 2082, introduced to the House of Representatives by the Ministry of Industry, Commerce and Supplies, represents the most significant step Nepal has taken on this issue in its legislative history.

For the first time, the Bill formally recognises Geographical Indications as a distinct and independent category of intellectual property, separated from trademarks, patents, and copyrights. It defines a geographical indication as a sign or geographical name that identifies goods originating from a particular region, where a specific quality, reputation, or characteristic is essentially attributable to that geographical origin.

That definition aligns Nepal, for the first time, with the international standard set by the TRIPS Agreement and with the domestic frameworks of countries that have used GI law to transform indigenous heritage into protected and profitable market assets. The Bill also proposes establishing an Industrial Property Office to administer GI registration and includes provisions to prevent unfair competition and the deceptive use of geographical names.

But the government cannot afford to wait for enactment before beginning the preparatory work that will determine whether the new law has anything meaningful to protect. The most urgent task Nepal faces right now is not legislative. It is documentary. Before a single GI application can be filed, before a single product can be examined and registered, the evidence base must exist.

Geographic boundaries must be mapped. Traditional production methods must be recorded. Community histories of origin must be compiled. Product quality standards must be defined. This work must begin immediately, in parallel with the Bill's parliamentary passage, so that the moment the law creates a registration mechanism, Nepal's producers are ready to use it.

The government must launch a National Traditional Knowledge Documentation Initiative without delay, coordinated across the Ministry of Culture, Tourism and Civil Aviation, the Ministry of Industry Commerce and Supplies, the Ministry of Agriculture, Forest and Environment, the Indigenous Nationalities Commission, and the National Foundation for Development of Indigenous Nationalities and Local Governments. This cannot be the work of one ministry acting alone. It requires field research, community consultation, geographic mapping, agricultural science, and legal analysis to work together systematically across all 59 indigenous nationalities and all ecological zones.

Non-governmental organisations and international NGOs working across Nepal's communities are essential partners in this effort and must be actively mobilised. They are already present in the villages where Dhaka is woven, in the tea gardens where Ilam farmers work, in the high-altitude communities where Yarsagumba is harvested, and in the community where Yomari is traditionally made.

Their field presence, community relationships, and research capacity can reach where government agencies cannot. WIPO’s traditional knowledge documentation guidelines provide a ready methodological framework that NGOs and research institutions can apply immediately. Local governments, empowered under Nepal’s federal structure, must also be formally directed and adequately resourced to participate.

What is needed now is the urgency to act, the coordination to document, and the institutional commitment to implement before the opportunity closes.

title: The Nepal floods question: When the Himalayas collapse, who gets warned? - Al Jazeera
description: The Nepal floods question: When the Himalayas collapse, who gets warned?  Al JazeeraNepal to use new flood study to claim millions from UN climate disaster fund  BBCScientists Warn of Flood Risks to 8 Himalayan Countries after Nepal Disaster  The New York Times
publisher.title: Al Jazeera
full_article:
New Delhi, India – On the morning of August 26, the Himalayan landscape above Nepal’s Rasuwa district changed in minutes.

A mass of ice and rock broke loose high in the mountains and sent a violent surge of water, mud and debris down the Lhende Khola River. The torrent travelled through valleys, swept away settlements and infrastructure and eventually reached the Nepal-China border.

What followed was not simply a flood.

It was a chain reaction.

By mid-September, more than 1,400 people had been reported dead and at least 6,000 remained missing in Nepal and across the border in Tibet. Twelve hydropower plants were destroyed, while roads, bridges and homes were buried or washed away.

The scale of the destruction has left scientists and disaster managers confronting a difficult question: How do you warn communities about a disaster whose trigger may occur high above them, in terrain that is difficult to monitor and where there may be only minutes to react?

Basanta Raj Adhikari, director of the Centre for Disaster Studies at Tribhuvan University in Kathmandu, described the event to Al Jazeera as unprecedented in size, affected area and mechanism. His estimate suggested that the energy involved was greater than that released by the Hiroshima atomic bomb, a comparison intended to illustrate the scale of the physical forces involved rather than suggest that the event was equivalent to a nuclear explosion.

For scientists who study the Himalayas, the disaster demonstrated how quickly an event originating in a remote, high-altitude environment can become a regional catastrophe.

Advertisement

And Nepal is not alone.

The warning problem

A warming climate is altering glaciers, snow cover, permafrost and high-altitude lakes. At the same time, roads, hydropower projects, tourist facilities and settlements have pushed deeper into mountain valleys.

That combination is creating a new risk landscape in which one hazard can trigger another.

An avalanche can block a river. A blocked river can form a temporary lake. A sudden release can become a debris flow. That debris can destroy a road or bridge, block another river and create another flood downstream.

The August disaster in Nepal showed how quickly such a sequence can unfold. It also exposed a weakness in the way early-warning systems are often designed.

Many systems are built around a particular hazard: rainfall, river level or glacial lake outburst flood. But the Himalayas do not always respect those categories.

In July, the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development, or ICIMOD, warned that a below-normal monsoon should not be interpreted as a safer one.

“The biggest misunderstanding is that less seasonal rainfall means lower flood risk,” said Saswata Sanyal, a disaster risk reduction specialist at ICIMOD.

“A drier monsoon can still be a dangerous monsoon,” he added, warning that seasonal averages cannot capture the cloudbursts capable of producing catastrophic flooding in mountain valleys.

The Nepal disaster went a step further.

The immediate trigger was not simply heavy rainfall.

Scientists have been examining an ice-rock avalanche and other possible processes that temporarily obstructed the river system before releasing a destructive surge. ICIMOD has described the event as an ice avalanche rather than a conventional glacial lake outburst flood, while other scientists have examined the role of local seismic activity and other high-altitude processes.

That distinction matters.

A warning system waiting for rainfall or a rising river may not provide enough time when the real trigger happens several kilometres upstream and above the line of sight of the communities below.

Indian National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) personnel conduct a search and rescue operation at the site of a flash flood at a village in the Kishtwar district of Indian-administered Kashmir on August 16, 2025 [AFP]

Kashmir’s warning signs

Thousands of kilometres away, scientists studying Kashmir’s Himalayas are seeing another part of the same problem.

A study published in the Journal of Glaciology this year mapped 155 glacial lakes above 2,500 metres (8,200ft) across the Himalayas in Indian-administered Kashmir.

Advertisement

The researchers found that the area of ice-contact proglacial lakes – bodies of water that form directly against the margin of a melting glacier, trapped by moraine ridges, bedrock basins, or ice dams – had increased by 26 percent between 1992 and 2024.

Five lakes were classified as having very high susceptibility to glacial lake outburst floods.

An outburst from those lakes, the researchers found, could threaten several thousand buildings, 15 major bridges, roads and a hydropower project.

More significantly, the study warned that hazards could occur in chains, with an upstream lake outburst potentially triggering secondary events downstream.

For Irfan Rashid, a glaciologist and associate professor at the University of Kashmir who co-authored the study, the implications extend beyond individual lakes.

Rashid recently told Al Jazeera that without action, the melting, thinning, and destabilisation of glaciers, seasonal snow cover, and permafrost along the Hindu Kush-Himalayas system would increase, and water shortages could become a major problem across the Upper Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra basins by the end of the century.

That is why the Nepal disaster resonates in Kashmir.

The landscapes are different, the rivers are different and the individual hazards may differ. But the underlying problem is increasingly similar: Communities living downstream of a rapidly changing high-altitude environment may have little time to respond when something breaks loose above them.

The challenge is particularly acute in places where roads, bridges and hydropower projects occupy narrow valleys.

Once a mountain river begins carrying enormous quantities of rock, ice and mud, infrastructure designed for conventional floods can quickly become irrelevant.

Volunteers rescue flood-affected victims along with their livestock using a boat following heavy rains and overflowing of the Sutlej River, on the outskirts of Multan in Punjab province, Pakistan, on September 4, 2025 [Shahid Saeed Mirza/AFP]

Pakistan has already begun building a warning network

The same concern runs across the western Himalayas and Karakoram ranges.

The Gilgit-Baltistan region in Pakistan-administered Kashmir contains hundreds of glaciers and glacial lakes, while communities and infrastructure sit along valleys exposed to sudden floods and landslides.

Pakistan has responded by expanding early-warning infrastructure.

Under a United Nations-supported programme, early-warning systems, evacuation shelters, disaster-management centres and other protective measures have been established in vulnerable valleys.

But technology alone cannot solve the problem. A sensor can detect a change. Someone still has to receive the message. Someone has to understand what it means. And people downstream have to have a route to safety.

That last part is often the weakest link. A siren is useful only if the people hearing it know where to go. An automatic warning is useful only if it arrives before the flood. A satellite image is useful only if the information can be converted into a decision quickly enough to save lives.

Advertisement

This is why disaster scientists increasingly talk about anticipatory action rather than simply disaster response.

“The era of preparing for a single, predictable hazard is over,” Sanyal said earlier this year. “Anticipatory action and early warning must now be the foundation.”

Nepal army soldiers work during a search and rescue operation outside a tunnel near a hydropower project site, following deadly flash floods and mudslides, in Rasuwa district, Nepal, on September 1, 2026 [Reuters]

The infrastructure trap

The Himalayas are also becoming more heavily engineered.

Hydropower is central to Nepal’s economy. Roads are being expanded. Border crossings are growing in importance. Tourism is pushing deeper into remote valleys.

The benefits are obvious. So are the risks.

The August disaster struck an area where hydropower infrastructure was concentrated along the river corridor. At least 900 workers were believed to have been inside tunnels and other facilities in the aftermath, making rescue operations extraordinarily difficult. Two workers were eventually pulled alive from a hydropower tunnel nine days after the disaster.

The question is no longer simply whether infrastructure can withstand a flood. It is whether planners have adequately considered what happens when a flood is carrying an enormous mass of rock and ice, when a river changes course, or when one mountain hazard triggers another.

For decades, engineering risk assessments have often relied on historical records. But history becomes a less reliable guide when the physical conditions producing disasters are changing.

A river that flooded once every several decades may no longer behave according to the same pattern. A glacier that appeared stable from satellite imagery may sit beneath an increasingly unstable slope. A lake that was considered remote may suddenly become a threat to a road, village or power plant hundreds of metres below.

Relatives of victims and missing people react outside the morgue of the Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital (TUTH), in Kathmandu, Nepal, August 29, 2026 [Narendra Shreshtha/EPA]

The border problem

There is another complication that no satellite can solve on its own.

Borders.

The Himalayas are divided among countries with different political systems, security concerns and approaches to sharing information. But rivers do not stop at international boundaries. Neither do floods.

The August disaster reached the Nepal-China border and damaged the Gyirong crossing, an important trade and pilgrimage route. The disaster also raised questions about how quickly information about hazards in high mountain areas can move between countries.

This is where regional cooperation becomes more than a diplomatic slogan, experts say. A sensor positioned in one country can provide warning to people in another. A satellite image collected over one mountain range can reveal a developing hazard that threatens a valley downstream. A river gauge can provide critical information before floodwaters reach a settlement.

The technical capability already exists in many cases. The missing piece is often the architecture connecting it.

A 2026 assessment of Himalayan disaster risks has argued for stronger monitoring, early-warning systems and regional coordination because hazards are increasingly interconnected.

The idea is simple: Information about a mountain hazard should not stop at the same line where a political boundary begins.

Buildings are inundated after flash floods triggered by sudden heavy rainfall swamped Rangpo town in Sikkim, India, Friday, October 6, 2023 [Prakash Adhikari/AP Photo]

From Nepal to Sikkim to Kashmir

The August disaster in Nepal isn’t a tragedy belonging to one country, point out experts.

Advertisement

The Kashmir Himalayas study has already identified lakes capable of producing destructive outburst floods and has warned of cascading processes.

Northeast India’s Sikkim provides another example.

After the 2023 South Lhonak glacial lake outburst flood killed dozens and damaged major infrastructure, India expanded monitoring and mitigation efforts.

Today, 40 high-risk glacial lakes have been identified in Sikkim, including 16 placed in the highest-risk category, with authorities working on drainage, flood-retention and other protective measures.

But the lesson from each disaster is broadly the same: Waiting for a disaster to prove the risk is the most expensive form of preparedness.

The world’s second largest mountain, the 8,611-metre- (28,251ft-) high K2 (seen in the distance), and the 8,051-meter- (26.414ft-) high Broad Peak (R), are illuminated by the moon at Concordia, the confluence of the Baltoro and Godwin-Austen glaciers, in the Karakoram mountain range in Pakistan, September 7, 2014 [Wolfgang Rattay/Reuters]

The Third Pole test

The Himalayas are sometimes called the Third Pole because they contain one of the world’s largest concentrations of snow and ice outside the Arctic and Antarctic.

Major Asian rivers depend on water originating in these mountains. Hundreds of millions of people live downstream.

That makes the changing Himalayas not only an environmental issue but a security, infrastructure and humanitarian one.

The August disaster demonstrated the most frightening version of that future. A mountain can collapse without warning. A river can become a weapon of debris. A hydropower tunnel can become a trap. A border crossing can disappear in minutes. And by the time people downstream understand what is happening, the water may already be there.

It’s a future that a region stretching from northeast India, spanning Tibet, Nepal, Kashmir and Pakistan, can no longer ignore. Yet disaster management remains largely divided by national boundaries. That contradiction is becoming harder to navigate.

The next glacial collapse could begin in Kashmir. It could begin in Pakistan’s high mountains. It could begin in Sikkim, Nepal or Tibet.

Wherever it starts, the same question will follow the mountain downstream: Who knew, how early did they know, and did the warning reach the people in time?

For a region entering an era of increasingly complex mountain hazards, that may be the real measure of whether the Third Pole is prepared.

title: Drums, dancing and definitely no tears: Here’s why you need to experience Nepal’s Sa: Paru festival - euronews.com
description: Drums, dancing and definitely no tears: Here’s why you need to experience Nepal’s Sa: Paru festival  euronews.com
publisher.title: euronews.com
full_article:
The sound I most associate with death is silence. Not just the obvious one, in that the dearly departed will never speak, never yell, never cry, never laugh again.

ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT

Smaller silences, like post-funeral, when the last guest is gone and all you’re left with are your thoughts and an inordinate amount of food shared by well-wishers. Or when weeks have passed and you go to call or text them about your day before you stop yourself because you can’t do that any more.

Even years later, it lingers in that awkward pause when you reveal someone close to you has passed away and the other person doesn’t quite know what to say in response.

Drums and bells, it is not. Music, beyond the songs chosen for the service, feels incongruous. The loud, chaotic energy of a festival? Never.

Yet that’s exactly what Sa: Paru, an annual festival honouring those that have died in the past year, is all about, as I discovered on my recent trip to Nepal’s Bhaktapur.

Celebrated across the Kathmandu Valley by the Newar people, the festival turns the western idea of grieving on its head, giving the dead a joyous farewell as they head towards salvation.

“When people pass away in western societies, people wear black. They grieve in silence – it's a very somber moment,” says Ajay Bahadur Pradhanang. “But in Nepal, everybody comes together and it's turned into this carnival, a real joyous moment of farewell.”

Bamboo structures known as taha: sa are created for the procession through the city Dianne Apen-Sadler

A community coming together

While the festival also takes place in other cities like Lalitpur as well as the capital Kathmandu, which is around 13 kilometres away, the celebration in Bhaktapur takes its own unique form.

Prior to the festival’s main day, which takes place after the full moon during the 10th month of the country’s lunisolar calendar in August or September, neighbours – whether they’ve lost someone or not – gather to create taha: sa.

The bamboo structures, which replaced the cows that would traditionally have been used as part of the procession, are wrapped before a painting of the sacred animal is placed at the top.

It takes skill, and manpower, to complete the whole affair. After the cloth (generally red for women, and white for men) and cow portrait are added, various decorations follow, like a photograph of the deceased, depictions of Shiva, and, finally, an umbrella to shield them from sun and rain – a sign of respect.

“For Sa: Paru, we have to have certain rituals, and these would be impossible if it was just me, or just my family, without the wider community to help us,” Ajay notes.

It might take a village to raise a child, but the celebration in Bhaktapur goes to show that it takes a community to mark the other end of somebody’s life, too.

I’m here at the invitation of The Nanee, a boutique hotel near the city’s centre. Ajay, the hotel’s chairman, lost his mother this year, which means I can see the work underway in the neighbouring courtyard, but any visitor to the city will easily be able to find taha: sa being constructed throughout the day.

The city gets busier and busier as the day goes on Dianne Apen-Sadler

The festival starts early the following morning, with a steady stream of taha: sa passing through the streets accompanied by music, drums, bells and the sound of sticks clashing together as pairs take part in the Ghintang Ghisi dance.

The procession follows a set route, and at the beginning, it seems each troupe is moving to its own beat – some rush, causing the structures to sway, giving the effect of a drunken cow passing by; others march slowly, pausing to dance together. It’s only as the streets begin to clog up and movement reaches a snail’s pace that they move as one.

While some attendees don traditional wear, or modern interpretations of it, you’re just as likely to see people wearing football kits and Hawaiian shirts. Come as you are – you’re welcome to get involved in the festivities, provided you don’t mind crowds.

After taking a pause to catch my breath, I get chatting to Mano Dhaubhadel, a Nepali living in the US who recently lost his younger brother and has returned for the festival.

“This is something you don’t see anywhere else in the world,” he told me. “The culture here is just magnificent, and it’s there for everyone to enjoy, not just Newars. The best way to learn is to get involved.”

Of course, you can also attend the festival with a guide. I’m joined by The Nanee’s curator, Peepul Subedi, a priest and PhD student who is more than happy to explain the meaning behind the festival’s various elements, and its importance.

"The whole city comes together for this festival, and every household who has a family member who has passed away in the past year will take out this sort of structure,” he tells me.

“It represents the message that everyone has to die, and all of us are going through the same sort of sorrow – that's life. We're not celebrating death by dancing and singing, we are celebrating the fact that the departed soul is moving towards salvation.”

Celebrations in most of the valley last just a single day – here in Bhaktapur, the festival continues on for eight, with different dance performances throughout the city.

The exact origins of Sa: Paru, which is also known as Gai Jatra, aren’t precisely known, but historians believe that the tradition may have started in the 14th century.

The name most commonly associated with the festival is King Pratap Malla, who is said to have expanded the festival to cheer up his wife following the death of their son Chakravartendra Malla with the inclusion of satirical elements, which today sees people don satirical masks of political figures like US president Donald Trump and Russian president Vladimir Putin.

Many tourists pass through Bhaktapur on a day trip – but there are plenty of reasons you should linger longer Dianne Apen-Sadler

A reason to linger in Bhaktapur

Travel itineraries for tourists visiting Kathmandu often include a detour to Bhaktapur – but they typically only mention a visit to the Durbar Square, with its various temples and the 55 Window Palace.

Similar to the cruise ship tourists who swarm cities in Europe for a few hours in the summer months, climbing back on board having contributed nothing to the local economy beyond the cost of an ice cream and a fridge magnet, these visitors will spend an hour or two in town before heading back to the capital.

It’s a real shame – not just for the locals, who fail to see the financial benefit, but for the tourists themselves, who miss out on the best Bhaktapur has to offer.

Life is slower here, and the city is best experienced in the early mornings, when you’ll see folks milling about, praying at the Hindu and Buddhist temples, or buying produce at the market.

Aside from the Durbar Square, you can see ceramics drying under the sun at Pottery Square, give pottery a go yourself at one of the workshops, or pick out some pieces to add to your homeware collection.

The Nanee aims to be an oasis of calm within the city of Bhaktapur Dianne Apen-Sadler

The Peacock Shop is another must visit, where the chatty owner is more than happy to talk, and walk you through the traditional Lokta paper making process.

The Nanee was founded by Ajay and Shailaja Pradhanang with a view to encourage people to linger longer while enjoying the comforts of a luxury boutique hotel.

“Bhaktapur is a living heritage site, and we wanted that to continue,” Ajay tells me.

“With The Nanee, we offer guests a small oasis in the beautiful city of Bhaktapur while ensuring that the community, which has done so much to preserve and conserve its heritage, benefits from their stay.”

Experiences offered by the hotel are in partnership with locals, like the morning walk with a housewife, or the evening dinner with an artisan.

Aside from Sa: Paru, there are numerous festivals throughout the year, including the famed Bisket Jatra, celebrated for eight nights each April.

A note on the recent floods

Just hours before landing in Kathmandu for the festival, a series of flash floods near the border with Tibet saw the loss of at least 1,369 lives, with some 5,000 people missing.

Naturally, many people have cancelled or are thinking about cancelling their trips to Nepal as a result, which will have a serious impact on a tourism industry that is already dealing with the impact of the Iran war on flight routes to the country.

Popular tourist spots like the Kathmandu Valley, as well as Mount Everest and other trekking trails, were unaffected by the tragedy, and your tourism dollars are more needed than ever.

title: Unfinished Democratic Journey Of Nepal - The Rising Nepal
description: Unfinished Democratic Journey Of Nepal  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
As we celebrate Constitution Day today, it is important for all Nepali citizens to pause and reflect on what our history has been, where we are now and where we need to head. The current Constitution, adopted in 2015, transformed Nepal into a federal democratic republic. At present, the government is taking forward a process to amend the Constitution. Before doing so, however, it is important to understand its strengths and weaknesses and the impact any amendment could have on the country. One of its biggest strengths is the provision of equal rights and access for all citizens through a federal republic. If amendments are needed, they should strengthen the implementation of people's rights and ensure freedom of the press, without which there can be no democracy. If people are still unable to access their rights because of their gender or marginalised situation, or if press freedom is curtailed in the name of sovereignty or individual privacy, such provisions should be amended. Before amending the Constitution, however, let us understand our history and recognise the strengths of what we have achieved.

Over the last 85 years, Nepal has had a revolutionary struggle between the royals and the people to institutionalise democracy. The country finally emerged from absolute monarchy to a federal republic in 2008, but the mindset of lawmakers and the general public still appears dominated by patriarchal and feudal thinking. During these eight decades, Nepal has witnessed the fall and rise of dynasties, the rewriting of constitutions several times and progress in laws addressing marginalised communities and gender disparities. Implementation, however, has remained a struggle.

There have also been positive outcomes. Nepal is one of the few countries on earth where visitors filling visa forms have the option of “other” alongside “male” and “female”. The same option exists for citizenship and voter IDs. Gender parity indicators also show Nepal climbing the ladder. Yet, when we consider impunity in addressing gender justice and the rights of people affected by civil wars and other injustices, the dreams of Nepali people in a federal republic are yet to be fully realised. This journey has faced further challenges from climate change, earthquakes, floods, changes in food cultivation and trade, and time after time economic embargoes. Nepal's landlocked geography and its geopolitical position between two giant neighbours and within a wider global power structure remain an ongoing reality. The Gen Z revolution of 2025 can be seen as a passive volcano that erupted and shook the country with a hope that peace and stability will now be established.

The social fabric of Nepal consists of an accepted culmination of Buddhist and Brahminic Hindu traditions, intermingled through festivals and events based on legendary anecdotes. This remarkable synthesis has developed between two related but divergent value systems. From being the only Hindu country on earth, Nepal is now a secular country where Muslim, Christian and other religious communities remain minorities. Recent incidents where this very harmony has been disturbed by unfortunate incidents that were fortunately resolved peacefully. However, attention needs to be given on how to make sure such sentiments do not arise again.

On this Constitution day we need to reflect on the historical and revolutionary fact of federal Nepal is the current electoral system and provision that two ward members in each ward must be women, one of them a Dalit woman. With 6,743 wards across the country, this means at least 13,486 women, including at least 6,743 Dalit women. The Election Commission also mandates that 40.4 per cent of nominees be women, including a rule requiring the chief and deputy chief nominations put forward by each political party in each local unit to be gender-even.

The proportional representation and first-past-the-post electoral systems in Nepal are envisioned to ensure equal representation. Unfortunately, both systems, especially the proportional representation system, are often manipulated. If the Constitution is to be amended, both systems need to be retained, but strict provisions should be made to prevent their manipulation based on political party interests.

The first local elections held in Nepal in 2017 therefore resulted in at least one woman occupying one of the top two positions at every level of municipalities and wards. In the 2022 elections, women held 33.09 per cent of seats in the national Parliament, in line with the constitutional provision. Women elected at local levels accounted for 41.21 per cent in 2022, compared with 40.9 per cent in 2017. This in itself has set a record for the highest number of women politicians in local governance systems in South Asia.

Yet the protests by some of Nepal's youngest population in 2025 speak volumes about the need to do more. Political leaders and mainstream political parties that played key roles in driving the monarchy away have faced accusations in several cases of corruption and crimes against humanity. After the Gen Z uprising and the uprooting of the KP Oli-led government in early September 2025, political leaders were shaken. As the days have gone by, a youth-led government has been trying to make a change and establish good governance, while the older political parties are slowly returning to their former stage.

There was speculation that the younger generation within parties such as the United Marxist Leninist Party (UML), Nepali Congress and Maoist parties would move into senior positions, but this has not happened so far. Even with a youth-led, educated government with almost a two-thirds majority in Parliament, there are often hurdles. One reason speculated for this is its commitment to bringing justice against corruption and addressing the lack of impunity that has continued for decades after the restoration of democracy in 1990.

The Constitution has given Nepal a federal democratic framework and recognised many rights that were once denied or ignored. But a Constitution is not realised merely by writing rights into a document. The real test lies in whether those rights reach every citizen, whether freedom of the press is protected, whether marginalised communities receive justice and whether impunity is ended. As we mark Constitution Day, we therefore need to pause, reflect on what our history has been, recognise where we are now and ask ourselves where we need to head. The journey is not yet complete.

(Sharma is a senior journalist and rights advocate. namrata1964@yahoo.com X handle: NamrataSharmaP)

title: Nepal leaders call for stronger governance, inclusion on Constitution Day - kathmandupost.com
description: Nepal leaders call for stronger governance, inclusion on Constitution Day  kathmandupost.com
publisher.title: kathmandupost.com
full_article:
Nepal marked Constitution Day and National Day on Saturday, with the country’s top state officials and political leaders calling for stronger governance, social justice, inclusion and fuller implementation of the constitution.

In a message marking the day, President Ramchandra Paudel said the constitution’s vision of a federal democratic republic should help deliver lasting peace, good governance and prosperity. He also called for unity and solidarity in responding to the loss of life and property caused by the August 26 Bhotekoshi floods .

“The Constitution envisions an equitable society based on social justice and an economy oriented towards socialism underpinned by democratic values,” Paudel said, stressing equal access to state services and social security.

Vice President Ramsahay Prasad Yadav also called for greater commitment to inclusion, equality and proportional representation, describing the constitution as a product of the Nepali people’s long struggle and the country’s diversity.

Prime Minister Balendra Shah, addressing a Constitution Day ceremony in Kathmandu, said his government was committed to both the letter and spirit of the constitution. But he warned that even a strong constitution could become “just a piece of paper” if those implementing it were not honest and committed.

Shah said the government was pursuing administrative reform, zero tolerance for corruption, political neutrality in the bureaucracy and merit-based appointments to public office. He also said his government would prioritise artificial intelligence, innovation and a knowledge-based economy.

Rastriya Swatantra Party chair Rabi Lamichhane said any review of the constitution should focus on people at the margins of society. Calling it a ‘sacred contract’ between the state and citizens, he said its guarantee of fundamental rights must be reflected in the daily lives of marginalised people.

Former prime minister KP Sharma Oli, who leads the CPN-UML, and former prime minister Pushpa Kamal Dahal, coordinator of the Nepali Communist Party, also called for protecting the constitution and its gains. Oli urged constitutional forces to unite to safeguard the charter and strengthen national unity, while Dahal said its achievements must be linked to people’s daily lives and its unfinished tasks completed.

India’s External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Pakistani President Asif Ali Zardari also extended greetings to Nepal on the occasion.

title: Nepal flood disaster exposes gaps in cross-border early-warning systems - The Business Standard

full_article:
A massive ice and rock avalanche in Nepal's Rasuwa district in late August sent water, mud and debris down the Lhende Khola River towards the Nepal-China border, highlighting weaknesses in disaster early-warning systems across the Himalayan region.

By mid-September, more than 1,400 people were reported dead and at least 6,000 remained missing across Nepal and Tibet. The disaster destroyed 12 hydropower plants and buried or swept away homes, roads and bridges, says Al Jazeera.

Experts say the scale and speed of such events expose limitations in warning systems that are often designed around individual hazards, such as rainfall or rising river levels, rather than sequences of events that can develop rapidly in high-altitude terrain.

Limits of existing warning systems

Traditional early-warning systems generally focus on hazards that can be monitored through indicators such as rainfall totals or river levels. But Himalayan disasters can involve several stages, including ice-rock avalanches, landslides or seismic activity that blocks a river before a sudden release sends a surge downstream.

Communities below may have only minutes to respond once a high-altitude trigger occurs beyond their line of sight.

Saswata Sanyal, a disaster risk reduction specialist at ICIMOD, said below-normal seasonal rainfall should not be interpreted as meaning flood risks are lower, because localised cloudbursts can still produce destructive flash floods.

The risks are also not confined to Nepal. The Himalayas hold one of the world's largest concentrations of snow and ice outside the polar regions and feed major river systems on which hundreds of millions of people depend.

In Kashmir, glaciologist Irfan Rashid has warned that glacial lake outburst floods could threaten thousands of buildings, 15 major bridges, roads and hydropower facilities. Changes involving glaciers, seasonal snow and permafrost could also contribute to major water shortages across the Upper Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra basins by the end of the century.

In Sikkim, authorities identified 40 high-risk glacial lakes after the 2023 South Lhonak glacial lake outburst flood, which killed dozens of people. Sixteen of those lakes were placed in the highest-risk category for mitigation efforts.

In Pakistan's Gilgit-Baltistan, hundreds of glaciers and glacial lakes leave communities in mountain valleys exposed to sudden flooding and landslides.

Infrastructure under pressure

The risks are compounded by extensive development in narrow mountain valleys, where hydropower facilities, roads, border trade routes and tourism infrastructure have expanded.

Infrastructure designed to withstand conventional flooding can be overwhelmed when rivers carry large quantities of rock, mud and ice, experts say.

During the August disaster, at least 900 workers were trapped inside hydropower tunnels and facilities. Two workers were rescued alive after being trapped for nine days.

The incident underscored the exposure of critical infrastructure in valleys where there can be little time to evacuate workers or protect facilities once a high-altitude collapse occurs.

Need for cross-border warnings

The movement of rivers and floodwaters across national boundaries presents another challenge.

Early-warning networks and data-sharing arrangements remain fragmented by national borders, with political and security concerns affecting the flow of information between countries.

The August flooding damaged the Gyirong border crossing between Nepal and China, highlighting the importance of communication between authorities on both sides of the border.

Experts say disaster management systems need to move beyond preparations for individual hazards and towards anticipatory action that accounts for interconnected and rapidly developing events.

That includes real-time cross-border data sharing and the establishment of warning systems before disasters occur.

The problem is particularly acute in the Himalayas, where natural hazards do not follow political boundaries. Rivers can cross several countries, while the region is divided among states with different political systems, security priorities and information-sharing arrangements.

Experts say disaster-management operations remain largely organised along national lines, even though a high-altitude collapse originating in Nepal, Tibet, Kashmir, Sikkim or Pakistan can have consequences beyond the country where it begins.

For communities downstream, delays in transmitting information can be critical. Disasters can originate in remote terrain and reach populated areas within minutes, leaving little time for evacuation.

Across the region stretching from northeast India and Tibet through Nepal, Kashmir and Pakistan, climate-driven changes are adding pressure to already vulnerable high-altitude environments.

Experts say a central test of regional preparedness is whether information can move faster than the flood: "Who knew, how early did they know, and did the warning reach the people in time?"

Nepal will give disaster early warning systems its highest priority, Prime Minister Balendra Shah said on Saturday, as the country grapples with the aftermath of devastating floods in the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river basins.

According to figures from Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, 1,410 bodies have been recovered and 6,055 people remain out of contact. Rescue teams have brought 13,756 people to safety.

Delivering his first Constitution Day address since taking office in March, Shah called for a stronger focus on reducing risks and preparing communities before disasters strike.

Shah said Nepal’s exposure to natural hazards demanded a proactive approach to disaster management.

“Special emphasis will be placed on risk reduction, preparedness, and response. Disaster early warning systems will be implemented with the highest priority,” he said.

The announcement comes as search and recovery operations continue following the August 26 flash flood, which struck riverside settlements in Rasuwa district and rapidly affected neighbouring areas, including Nuwakot and Dhading.

Of the 344 injured people admitted to hospitals, 290 have been discharged, according to the disaster authority.

The Nepal Army, Nepal Police and Armed Police Force mounted a large-scale response, with the deployment of security personnel exceeding 20,000 at one stage.

Helicopters evacuated critically injured people, pregnant women, children, elderly residents and people with disabilities. In Nuwakot, 611 people are being accommodated in temporary shelters at 13 locations.

Roads, Bridges and Power Projects Hit

The floods have also dealt a severe blow to transport links and energy infrastructure.

Eight operating hydropower projects with a combined capacity of 281 MW were damaged, along with four projects under construction representing another 388 MW.

Major stretches of the Galchhi–Betrawati–Rasuwagadhi road and the Prithvi Highway were destroyed or severely damaged. The disaster also damaged 48 suspension bridges and 31 motorable bridges.

Telecommunications services have been restored across 95 per cent of affected areas. Electricity restoration is progressing at different rates across the affected districts.

Authorities are carrying out immediate relief work alongside road restoration and bridge reconstruction.

Recovery and Identification Continue

The government has declared 15 local administrative areas disaster crisis-hit zones for three months and released money from the Prime Minister’s Relief Fund.

The fund has collected more than NPR 7 billion, in addition to foreign contributions.

Shah acknowledged assistance and messages of support from India, China, the United States, Japan and international institutions, including the Asian Development Bank, World Bank, European Union and United Nations.

Search operations continue for those still missing. Authorities are preserving DNA samples from unidentified bodies to support identification and help families establish the fate of their relatives.

The Constitution Day address placed disaster preparedness at the centre of the government’s response, as Nepal faces the immediate demands of rescue and relief alongside a prolonged reconstruction effort.

title: Nepal begins probe into what triggered Bhotekoshi disaster - kathmandupost.com
description: Nepal begins probe into what triggered Bhotekoshi disaster  kathmandupost.com
publisher.title: kathmandupost.com
full_article:
The Nepal government has commissioned a comprehensive scientific investigation into what triggered the devastating August 26 floods in Rasuwa, how the disaster unfolded and whether climate change played a role.

For the investigation, the Ministry of Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation has formed a seven-member panel of experts in hydrology, glaciology, geology, remote sensing, hydropower infrastructure and disaster risk reduction.

The panel will conduct field studies from the source of the disaster to the affected areas downstream, examining the geological, glacial and hydrological processes involved in the event, the ministry said.

The investigation follows a preliminary assessment that found insufficient scientifically verified evidence to establish where the disaster originated, what physical process triggered it or how the sequence of events spread downstream through the Bhotekoshi-Lhende river system.

The government wants to determine whether a sequence of geological, glacial and hydrological hazards in the high mountains triggered the disaster, rather than simply flooding or heavy rainfall.

“This is a rare event even by global standards. We cannot conclude without a detailed study,” said Tikaram Baral, joint secretary at the Water and Energy Commission Secretariat. “Once we have collected all the scientific evidence, an appropriate name will be given.”

The seven-member panel is coordinated by water policy and governance expert Debesh Belbase. Its members include hydrologist Narendra Man Shakya, glaciologist Rijan Bhakta Kayastha, remote-sensing expert Uttam Babu Shrestha, geologist Meghraj Dhital, hydropower infrastructure expert Hari Pandit and disaster-risk reduction specialist Anil Pokhrel.

The panel will also consider possible names for the disaster. Options discussed so far include “glacial rock avalanche”, “ice-rock avalanche/landslide” and “Rasuwa Bhotekoshi megadisaster”.

The study will examine geology, temperature and water systems together, as well as the possible role of climate change in the disaster, according to ministry spokesman Mohan Kumar Shakya.

The investigation is also intended to identify lessons for the energy sector. The Bhotekoshi disaster caused extensive damage along the Trishuli corridor, raising concerns about the vulnerability of hydropower infrastructure to similar events in other river systems.
